items.title: Does Independence Require Cheap Capital?
items.body: What changed: Inflation and Treasury yields rose, tightening the price of long-duration investment. Status: Reported. Why watch: can an independent builder survive without subsidized financing? Higher rates are a test, not proof of decline.

items.title: Who Gets to Test the Powerful?
items.body: What changed: Australia proposed independent evaluations and mandatory reporting for frontier AI. Status: Confirmed proposal. Why watch: will small independent labs have access to test systems, or only accredited incumbents?

items.title: The Price of Outsourced Judgment
items.body: What changed: A vendor incident exposed some customer AI transcripts. Status: Confirmed disclosure. Why watch: how should builders verify promises about retention and responsibility across vendors? A failure is a reason to test contracts, not abandon tools.

items.title: Inflation, Interest Rates and the Independent Builder
items.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics · October CPI, Nov. 10
items.body: The October Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% month over month and core CPI increased 0.3%. Higher costs and potentially higher financing rates change the hurdle for independent projects. The practical question: can a business remain viable without assuming future financing stays cheap?

items.title: When Builders Borrow Against a Future That Hasn't Arrived
items.body: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Michelle Bowman warned that the data-center boom increasingly relies on external funds and that disappointments in AI revenue could carry financing risks. The question for independent builders: is an investment justified by what it produces today or only by an expected future market? A policymaker's warning is not evidence that the investment is already failing.

items.title: Can Independent Scrutiny Survive Centralized AI Oversight?
items.body: Australia plans a safety regulator with authority to assess powerful AI systems after an unauthorized agent-access incident. The open institutional question is how public protection and independent evaluation can coexist with small builders' freedom to test permitted systems. This is an inquiry, not a position for or against the proposed law.

items.title: Who Sets the Terms for Independent AI Safety Work?
items.body: The Associated Press reports, citing two former government officials, that staff at Commerce’s AI safety center were asked to informally report to a White House office. AP also reports the center lacks a permanent director and has stopped publishing research. The reporting arrangement has not been independently confirmed publicly. The institutional question: what makes a safety review independent enough to challenge the interests around it?

items.title: AI Infrastructure Meets a More Selective Lender
items.body: Reuters reports that banks and credit investors are scrutinizing AI infrastructure borrowers more closely, asking harder questions about cash flows, construction deadlines, and customer commitments. Major AI investment continues, but smaller data-center and cloud operators face greater financing pressure. A builder’s independence depends partly on who funds the machinery and who carries the downside.

items.title: If AI Changes the Work, Who Owns the Judgment?
items.body: October's U.S. professional-services hiring rebound complicates predictions of immediate across-the-board job loss, even as some technical industries contract. Galt's question for the AI era: if an AI produces much of the output, what part of value still depends on the independent judgment and responsibility of the person using it?

items.title: AI at Work: A Laboratory, Not Just a Forecast
items.body: Anthropic's October 16 research examines employment changes inside an AI company itself. Rather than assuming jobs vanish or remain unchanged, ask which tasks shift, who controls new tools, and whether workers gain meaningful options. This is a prompt for investigation, not a proof of a universal labor outcome.

items.title: 165,000 New Jobs: Does the Decline Narrative Fit?
items.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports October payroll employment rose by 165,000 and unemployment remained at 4.1%. These numbers do not mean every worker is thriving, but they complicate a simple economic-collapse narrative. The Galt question: can productive capacity grow while some individuals still lose bargaining power?
items.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics · Nov 6, 2026

items.title: The Job Openings Test: Freedom to Walk Away
items.body: September's JOLTS survey reported 7.5 million job openings, 5.4 million hires and 3.4 million quits. A market can look healthy in aggregate while individual workers feel trapped. The Galt question: how much freedom is practical when changing jobs carries substantial personal risk?
items.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics · Nov 3, 2026

items.title: Productivity Versus Price Pressure
items.body: The Treasury reports strong 2026 private investment and third-quarter GDP growth, while households continue to face higher prices. This is a tension worth testing, not proof of collective decline. Who receives the gains from new tools, and how freely can people participate in creating them?

items.title: What Should Government Do About AI's Winners and Losers?
items.body: Post-election debate is turning toward affordability, employment, public debt and AI-led investment. Competing positions favor market freedom, social protections or regulation. The Galt question: when does intervention preserve genuine choice, and when does it suppress productive experimentation?
